lines.name: Level: B2+ · Topic: The Bicycle Shop

lines.text:
Two Wheels, One City — The Culture of Cycling

The bicycle shop on the corner is more than a retail space — it is a neighbourhood institution. Inside, road bikes with lightweight frames hang from ceiling hooks. Mountain bikes with thick tires and heavy-duty brakes line one wall. A row of hybrid models sits between them, designed for riders who split their time between bike lanes and unpaved trails. In the back, a mechanic tightens a chain with a wrench, replaces a worn brake pad, and inflates a flat tire with a floor pump.

The anatomy of a bicycle is deceptively simple. Two wheels connected by a frame, driven by pedals through a chain to the rear gear. Yet the engineering is precise: each spoke in the wheel must carry equal tension. The handlebar controls direction; the seat must sit at the correct height to protect the rider's knees. Brakes — whether rim, disc, or coaster — must respond instantly. A well-maintained gear system lets the rider climb a steep hill without exhausting effort or cruise downhill without losing control.

Cycling infrastructure has reshaped urban planning. Dedicated bike lanes now run through city centres, separated from motor traffic by physical barriers. Cyclists signal before every turn and stop at intersections. Cities like Amsterdam, Copenhagen, and Bogotá have invested in cycling paths that connect residential areas to workplaces, schools, and parks. Lock-up stations and bike racks outside shops encourage people to park securely and walk the final stretch.

Safety gear has evolved alongside the culture. A helmet remains the most important piece of equipment. Lights — front white, rear red — are legally required after dark in most countries. A reflective vest makes riders visible on poorly lit roads. Bells warn pedestrians; mirrors allow riders to check traffic behind them without turning. For longer rides, a water bottle, phone mount, and puncture repair patch kit are considered essential.

The market has diversified considerably. An electric bike appeals to commuters facing long distances or hilly terrain — a small motor assists the pedals without replacing them. A folding bike suits travellers who combine cycling with public transport. A cargo bike carries children or groceries in a front-mounted box. A tandem lets two people ride together. A cruiser — wide seat, swept-back handlebar — suits leisure riders along flat coastal paths. Even a BMX, once associated only with trick riding, has found a commuting audience among younger riders who value agility in traffic.

Cycling clothing has become technical. A jersey wicks sweat; padded shorts reduce friction on long rides. Gloves cushion the palms against road vibration. Cycling shoes clip into the pedals for efficient power transfer. Arm warmers and leg warmers add layered warmth without the bulk of a jacket. A cap worn under the helmet shields the eyes from sun and rain.

The bicycle shop mechanic uses specialised tools: a tire lever to remove the tire from the rim, a chain tool to break and rejoin links, a spoke wrench to true a wobbling wheel, and grease to keep moving parts silent. A multi-tool — combining hex keys, screwdrivers, and a bottle opener — fits in a jersey pocket for roadside repairs. The stand holds the bike at working height, allowing the mechanic to spin the wheel freely and diagnose problems by sound and sight.

lines.text: Scene: A customer visits a bicycle shop looking for their first commuter bike

lines.text: Hi, I'm looking for a bike for commuting — about ten kilometres each way. What would you recommend?
lines.name: Hi, I'm looking for a bike for commuting — about ten kilometres each way. What would you recommend?

lines.text: For commuting, a hybrid is your best bet. It has a sturdy frame, comfortable seat, and smooth gear shifts. Or an electric bike if you want less effort on hills.
lines.name: For commuting, a hybrid is your best bet. It has a sturdy frame, comfortable seat, and smooth gear shifts. Or an electric bike if you want less effort on hills.

lines.text: What's the difference between a road bike and a hybrid?
lines.name: What's the difference between a road bike and a hybrid?

lines.text: A road bike has thinner tires and a lighter frame — built for speed. A hybrid has wider tires, an upright handlebar, and better comfort for daily rides.
lines.name: A road bike has thinner tires and a lighter frame — built for speed. A hybrid has wider tires, an upright handlebar, and better comfort for daily rides.

lines.text: I'll try the hybrid. What accessories do I need?
lines.name: I'll try the hybrid. What accessories do I need?

lines.text: A helmet is essential. Then a lock, a front and rear light, and a bell. I'd also recommend a rack for your bag.
lines.name: A helmet is essential. Then a lock, a front and rear light, and a bell. I'd also recommend a rack for your bag.

lines.text: What about maintenance? I don't know much about bikes.
lines.name: What about maintenance? I don't know much about bikes.

lines.text: Keep the chain oiled, check the tire pressure with a pump weekly, and test the brake before every ride. Bring it in for a tune-up every few months.
lines.name: Keep the chain oiled, check the tire pressure with a pump weekly, and test the brake before every ride. Bring it in for a tune-up every few months.

lines.text: Do the pedals come with the bike, or do I choose separately?
lines.name: Do the pedals come with the bike, or do I choose separately?

lines.text: Standard pedals are included. If you want clip-in pedals, you'll need cycling shoes too. We also have gloves and a water bottle holder.

lines.text: 'By + transport' uses no article or possessive: 'by bicycle', 'by car', 'by train'. When you add 'my/the', switch to 'on': 'on my bicycle'. This zero-article rule after 'by' applies to all transport nouns and is a persistent source of errors even at B2+.

lines.text: Passive infinitive = 'to be + past participle': 'to be repaired', 'to be replaced'. An alternative pattern: 'needs + -ing' (active form, passive meaning): 'The bike needs repairing.' 'The chain needs replacing.' Both are correct; the -ing form is more informal.

lines.text: ❌ "He suggested me to buy a hybrid bike."
lines.name: ❌ "He suggested me to buy a hybrid bike."

lines.text: ✅ "He suggested (that) I buy a hybrid bike." / "He suggested buying a hybrid bike."
lines.name: ✅ "He suggested (that) I buy a hybrid bike." / "He suggested buying a hybrid bike."

lines.text: 'Suggest' never takes object + infinitive (*suggest me to buy). It takes: (1) suggest + (that) + subject + bare infinitive: 'He suggested I buy...' (2) suggest + -ing: 'He suggested buying...' (3) suggest + noun: 'He suggested a hybrid.' This pattern also applies to 'recommend', 'propose', and 'insist'.

lines.text: 'Since' = from a specific point in time: 'since 8 a.m.', 'since Tuesday', 'since I was ten.' 'For' = duration: 'for three hours', 'for two weeks', 'for a long time.' The since/for distinction with present perfect continuous is a B1+ staple that still produces errors at B2+.

lines.text: ✅ "Despite the rain, she cycled to work." / "In spite of the rain, she cycled to work."

lines.text: 'Despite' takes a noun directly — never 'despite of'. 'In spite of' takes a noun with 'of'. Despite = in spite of (interchangeable meaning, different grammar). 'Despite the hill, he kept riding.' 'In spite of the flat tire, she finished the race.' Mixing the two forms ('despite of') is a common B2 error.

lines.text: 'Bike' is the informal, everyday word. 'Bicycle' is more formal/technical. In conversation, nearly everyone says 'bike'. 'Bicycle' appears in formal writing, signs, and official documents. 'Motorbike' or 'motorcycle' is the powered two-wheeler — never just 'bike' unless context is clear.

lines.text: The Netherlands is the world's most bike-friendly country — with dedicated infrastructure, traffic lights for cyclists, and multi-storey bike parking. In the UK, cycling has grown rapidly but infrastructure still lags behind. 'Cycle to work schemes' let British employees buy bikes tax-free through their employer.

lines.text: British English: 'tyre' (rubber covering on a wheel). American English: 'tire'. Both are correct in their variety. Note: 'tire' in British English means to become weary — 'I tire of this argument.' This is a common spelling confusion for learners.

lines.text: The UK has no law requiring adults to wear cycle helmets — it's a personal choice, though strongly recommended. In Australia and New Zealand, helmets are compulsory. In the Netherlands and Denmark, almost nobody wears one because the cycling infrastructure is so safe. Different countries, different norms.
